# Exact sharp-product value of the continuous-normal hinge minimum

This calibrates the attained potential in
`candidate de8d1a3251731edd`. It is a theorem
about that potential on the known sharp product family, not a proof of
the mixed-integer conjecture for other bodies.

Let `n>=1,d>=1`, let `K` be a `d`-simplex of volume `v`, and put

`S={0,1}^n x K`, `M=2^n v`, `N=2^n(d+1)`.

Let `g` be the simplex centroid. Let `H_j` denote the altitude from
vertex `j` to its opposite facet, for `j=0,...,d`. To avoid a conflict
with the notation for ambient caps, altitude is written `H_j` only in
this note.

Among all covers by `N` closed ambient caps

`L_i(z,x)=a_i dot z+u_i dot x-b_i>=0`, `|u_i|=1`,

whose individual mixed masses are at most

`gamma_d v=2^(-n) gamma_d M`,

the hinge potential has the exact value

`Psi = M * d gamma_d/(d+1)^2 * sum_(j=0)^d H_j`.                (1)

In fact every such feasible cover has this value. For a regular simplex
of inradius `r`, all altitudes equal `(d+1)r`, so (1) becomes

`Psi=M d r gamma_d`.                                          (2)

## 1. Equality caps through the simplex centroid

A closed proper cap of `K` containing `g` has volume at least
`gamma_d v`. Equality forces its boundary to pass through `g`, and the
cap is the vertex cap parallel to the opposite facet.

Here are the needed equality details. If the centroid is strictly
inside the cap, translating its boundary to the centroid strictly
decreases the volume: the intermediate slabs meet the interior of `K`
in positive volume. Thus equality requires a boundary through `g`.
For `d>=2`, the proved simplex cap-gap theorem in
`candidate 191a0eb2244ea4a9` says that a
closed centroid cap containing at least two simplex vertices has
fraction at least `gamma_(d-1)>gamma_d`, including boundary vertices.
An equality cap therefore contains just one vertex, with strictly
positive functional value, and excludes every other vertex strictly.
Normalize its positive functional value to one. If the absolute values
at the other vertices are `b_1,...,b_d`, the centroid condition gives
`sum b_j=1`, and the exact cap fraction is

`product_(j=1)^d (1+b_j)^(-1)`.

This formula follows either from the simplex determinant for a
one-vertex cap or from independent exponential barycentric coordinates.
Arithmetic-geometric mean gives equality at `gamma_d` exactly when
all `b_j=1/d`. Hence the cutting plane is parallel to the opposite
facet. When `d=1`, the interval midpoint and its two half-intervals
give the same conclusion directly.

The simplex cap-gap note contains the full proof of the invoked strict
gap; no mixed-integer result is used in this step.

## 2. Every feasible cover consists of the canonical local caps

Fix a binary base vertex `p`. Any ambient cap containing `(p,g)` has
own-fiber mass at least `gamma_d v`, by Section 1. Its total cap budget
forces equality in that own fiber and zero mass in every other fiber.
It cannot contain any other fiber centroid, because that would add
another `gamma_d v>0` to its mass.

Thus every cap containing `(p,g)` is one of the `d+1` canonical
facet-parallel centroid cuts on that fiber. All other caps strictly
miss `(p,g)`, and, since there are finitely many caps, miss a whole
neighborhood of it in the fiber. Consequently the canonical cuts that
contain `(p,g)` must themselves cover a neighborhood of `g`.

All `d+1` vertex types are necessary. In barycentric coordinates,
such a cut has the form `lambda_j>=1/(d+1)`. If one type is missing,
decrease all coordinates of the present types by a small common amount
and add their total decrease to a missing coordinate. This gives an
interior point arbitrarily close to `g` that misses every present cut.

At least `d+1` caps therefore contain each `(p,g)`. No cap can serve two
such centroids. Since the total available cap count is exactly
`2^n(d+1)`, every cap serves exactly one centroid, and each fiber has
exactly one cap of each canonical type. This also proves that no cover
with fewer caps can meet this cap budget.

## 3. Exact hinge integration and feasibility

Let `lambda_j` be a barycentric coordinate on `K`, and put
`c=1/(d+1)`. Its gradient has norm `1/H_j`. The continuously normalized
canonical margin on its own fiber is therefore

`H_j(lambda_j-c)`.

Its hinge integral is

`v H_j integral_c^1 (1-t)^d dt
 =v H_j (d/(d+1))^(d+1)/(d+1)`.

It has zero hinge integral on every other fiber, because its cap there
has zero volume; a strictly positive hinge on a convex body's interior
would give positive cap volume. Summing these exact values over all
`2^n` fibers and all vertex types gives (1).

Finally the required covers exist with finite integer tilts. For every
binary vertex `p`, use the globally affine function

`q_p(z)=sum_k[(1-p_k)z_k+p_k(1-z_k)]`

and take, with any `A>1`, the caps

`lambda_j(x)-c-A q_p(z)>=0`.

On integer fibers they meet only fiber `p`, where their union covers
all of `K` by `max_j lambda_j>=c`. Each cap has mass `gamma_d v`.
Dividing its defining affine function by `|grad lambda_j|` gives the
required unit continuous normal. Thus the exact potential in (1) is
attained by actual closed ambient caps, including the common centroid
on their boundaries. QED.
